transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-07-28 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~47 minutes
- Attendees: Anna Lee (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood Product), Priya Rao (Lead ML Eng, Cobalt), Tom Beck (CTO, Cobalt), Maya Patel (SRE, Cobalt), Ethan Yu (PM, Cobalt)

[00:00] Anna Lee: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Anna from Redwood, this is Marcus and Luis, we'll run through the hosted chat playground and ops view, show streaming behavior, parameters you'll tune, and how retries work in practice.
[00:18] Priya Rao: Hi thanks, we wanted a fairly practical session — we have a prototype using a few open models, main asks are latency P95 under 300ms, and keeping cost predictable.
[00:32] Marcus Chen: Great, we'll try to address that. Quick agenda — short demo of the playground streaming, then console tour for metrics and Optimize hints, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:45] Tom Beck: Quick — can you also comment on private deployment options? If we go to production we may need VPC or on-prem for PHI.
[00:55] Luis Ortega: Absolutely, we'll touch on VPC and KMS later; hosted can support bring-your-own-key flows and private control planes for enterprise.

[02:12] Marcus Chen: Alright jumping into the playground — I'm creating a small chat session, model set to a 7B variant; for streaming you see partial tokens come through as they're generated.
[02:37] [screen share noises] Marcus Chen: Note the stream chunking strategy — we flush after sentence pieces typically, and we do delta events so client can render progressively.
[03:05] Maya Patel: Is there a way to control chunk size? Our UI is sensitive to too many small deltas.
[03:12] Marcus Chen: Yes, there's a stream coalescing parameter client-side and on the server we do batching heuristics. You can tune server flush thresholds via the console or pass streaming options in the SDK. It works with both websocket-style streams and SSE.

[05:01] Anna Lee: On generation params — temperature and top_p are the usual levers, also max_tokens and repetition_penalty for hallucination control. We'll show a few examples.
[05:28] Marcus Chen: Example 1: low temperature + top_p=0.9 for deterministic replies; Example 2: temp=0.9 for creative copy. Watch the playground as I change temp from 0.2 to 0.8 — streaming rate doesn't change much, but token choices do.
[06:10] Priya Rao: How does that affect cost? Randomness often increases tokens because of retries or longer outputs.
[06:20] Marcus Chen: Generally cost is proportional to tokens; higher temperature can produce longer outputs, but the bigger levers for cost are max_tokens and whether you use prefix caching. With repetition penalty and good prompts you can limit token bloat.

[08:00] Anna Lee: Now retries — common pattern is optimistic single-request with exponential backoff. Redwood's client libs include idempotency keys for requests; the hosted API can retry safely if you provide an idempotency token or mark messages as idempotent.
[08:22] Tom Beck: We have workflows that can't accept duplicate completions. How do you ensure dedup?
[08:30] Marcus Chen: Use idempotency keys and check the request status endpoint. For streaming, if a stream disconnects we recommend resuming with a continuation token rather than re-generating from scratch.
[08:44] Maya Patel: Is continuation token the same as KV cache pointer?
[08:49] Marcus Chen: They're related — we keep a small KV context pointer for the session which lets you resume without re-sending full history.

[10:15] Marcus Chen: Quick console tour — route dashboard shows per-route P50/P95, token breakdown (prompt vs completion), cost per token, and traces for individual requests. You can filter by model variant and region.
[10:42] [Marcus clicks] Marcus Chen: See here the Optimize tab? It suggests batching thresholds, whether quantization will be helpful for your model family, and recommends a cache TTL for common prefixes.
[11:05] Priya Rao: The batching suggestions — our traffic is bursty, how do you avoid added latency from batching?
[11:13] Marcus Chen: Optimize suggests sensible batch windows and we have latency SLO constraints — you can pin a max wait time. Redwood's runtime does continuous batching: it will batch requests that arrive within the small window but won't delay beyond the configured SLO. So you get cost reduction on background workloads and low latency for the rest.

[13:00] Tom Beck: For PHI we will probably need a private deployment. Can hosted satisfy any of the compliance requirements without private infra?
[13:08] Luis Ortega: Hosted can meet many compliance boxes — SOC 2 Type II, tenant isolation, and BYOK KMS for encryption at rest. For strict data residency or network isolation we offer Private (VPC) deployments or on-prem packages. We can share the compliance pack.
[13:28] Priya Rao: Do you support SSO? We use Okta.
[13:33] Anna Lee: Yes SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit logs are available in the enterprise bundle. We'll attach the security whitepaper.

[15:10] Marcus Chen: Back to retries — show a demo of a failed node: I'm simulating a dropped connection and then resuming the stream.
[15:23] [audio glitch] Marcus Chen: You can see the client call to resume with the last cursor; the server returns the remaining tokens. If the request failed before generation we automatically fallback to a smaller model variant if configured, to keep latency.
[15:50] Maya Patel: So fallback is per-route policy?
[15:54] Marcus Chen: Correct, you can set per-route policy: prefer low-latency path, or low-cost path, or strict model fidelity. Fallback can use quantized variants or smaller architecture.

[18:20] Ethan Yu: Any gotchas around token accounting when using KV caching? We want accurate cost reporting per session.
[18:28] Marcus Chen: Cached prefixes are only charged when the runtime materializes them into the prompt — console shows exact breakdown: cached vs non-cached tokens. There's also a TTL and cache hit rate metric in Optimize.

[20:00] Priya Rao: For the SDK, what's the pattern for streaming in mobile apps? We're worried about flaky cell networks.
[20:07] Marcus Chen: Use short-lived streams and resumable cursors, fallback to a synchronous API call in poor connectivity. We recommend idempotency keys and small chunk sizes. We also provide client-side coalescing to avoid UI jitter.

[22:10] Marcus Chen: I'll run a quick sample: code snippet in Node, open socket, on 'delta' event render partial, if socket closes send resume call with cursor.
[22:30] [Marcus pastes snippet] Marcus Chen: Note the header includes X-Idempotency-Key and X-Client-Cursor.

[25:01] Tom Beck: What about long-running conversations — do you recommend storing full history server-side, or relying on KV caches?
[25:12] Marcus Chen: A hybrid. Store canonical conversation in your DB for audit, but use prefix/KV cache for the hot context window to avoid re-sending full history and to improve latency. Cache eviction and TTL strategies are configurable.

[27:40] Anna Lee: Security specifics — we'll share SOC 2 report, we support BYOK KMS integrations and HSM for private deployments, SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning, and audit logs per request.
[28:00] Priya Rao: Any limits on BYOK? We need customer-managed keys for decryption in the VPC case.
[28:09] Luis Ortega: BYOK is supported; for VPC/private we can do a customer KMS endpoint or HSM in the private control plane. We'll include architecture diagrams in the security pack.

[30:55] Marcus Chen: Now let's look at an Optimize suggestion for their current workload; based on a few uploaded traces here the system suggests quantizing the 7B variant to int8 for ~40% cost drop with minimal quality delta for short-answer tasks.
[31:20] Priya Rao: Are there quality regression checks? We can't degrade answers for clinical triage.
[31:27] Marcus Chen: Yes, Optimize includes eval hooks where you can run your prompt test set and track scores. If quality drops beyond a threshold it flags and can auto-fallback to higher-fidelity model.

[33:10] Maya Patel: For the benchmark Marcus will send, what metrics should we capture?
[33:15] Marcus Chen: Capture P50/P95 latency, token cost per request, model quality on your eval set, throughput (req/sec) at target concurrency, and cache hit rate. We'll provide a small harness.

[35:00] [brief pause] Anna Lee: Let's recap — you wanted predictable P95 < 300ms and cost within X per month, evaluate hosted with a small pilot and run the 48-hour benchmark. We'll share pricing and security docs, vault/KMS details, and a sample bench notebook.

[36:12] Tom Beck: One more on procurement — any standard enterprise contract templates?
[36:18] Anna Lee: Yes we'll include the standard SOW and terms; for Private deployments procurement tends to add 4–6 weeks.

[38:40] [Q&A rapid fire]
[38:45] Priya Rao: If we do pilot and see latency spikes, what's the escalation path?
[38:50] Luis Ortega: Dedicated SLA for production tenants; during pilot we provide direct SE support and elevated routing. Also you can configure autoscale burst capacity for spikes.

[40:00] Ethan Yu: Will the playground allow us to test same traffic shape as prod?
[40:06] Marcus Chen: The playground is sample; for fidelity we'll provision a sandbox tenant with near-prod capacity for the benchmark.

[42:20] Anna Lee: Alright next steps — we'll send the docs, Marcus sends bench harness, schedule follow-up. Anything else from the Cobalt team?
42:33 Priya Rao: Nope that's good, thanks.
42:38 Tom Beck: Thanks all.

[43:00] Anna Lee: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the attachments.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional stutters and a few proper nouns misheard (e.g., "K V cash" for KV cache). Some timestamps approximate.
